clue.text: Without it, sailor may be a victim, sick with navy

definitions.text: Without it, sailor may be a victim, sick with navy

indicators.note: sick suggests the letters are in a bad way, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor of old, short of something vital, falls ill alongside the rest of the navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sick' is the anagram signal. The whole clue also describes the answer: on long voyages, sailors deprived of it fell victim to scurvy.
explanation.definitionFit: Scurvy comes from a lack of ascorbic acid, the classic deficiency disease of sailors at sea.

clue.text: Something troubling your eyelid primarily

indicators.note: primarily asks for the first letter of each of the four words before it

explanation.surface: A doctor's description of an irritation that mainly affects the eyelid.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the initials spell the word, and the clue describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small painful swelling on the edge of the eyelid is exactly something that troubles it.

clue.text: Fiddle with cross erected over court

indicators.note: the cross is placed over the court, covering it on both sides here
in a down clue, erected means the word is stood upright, read from bottom to top

parts.note: a rood is a crucifix or cross, as in a church rood screen

explanation.surface: Someone tinkers with a crucifix put up above a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erected' turns the cross upside down in this down entry, making DOOR, and 'over' wraps it round the court abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To fiddle accounts or figures is to falsify or tamper with them, a verb sense synonym.

clue.text: Part of Croydon or court in centre of Dundee

indicators.note: in places the other pieces inside the central pair
centre of takes the two middle letters of the six-letter city name

parts.note: taken as written
to court someone is to woo them

explanation.surface: A district of a London borough is set against a courtship in the middle of a Scottish city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of' takes the middle two letters of the six-letter Dundee, and 'in' splits them. Croydon is a borough of south London.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a district of south London lying largely within the borough of Croydon.

clue.text: Director, not quite 20, sees cast

indicators.note: not quite means the last letter of the word for twenty is dropped

parts.note: a score is twenty

indicators.note: cast in the sense of thrown about, so the letters of sees are rearranged

explanation.surface: A filmmaker, still a teenager, watches a cast at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' trims SCORE to SCOR; 'cast' rearranges SEES to SESE.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Scorsese is the celebrated American film director of Taxi Driver and Goodfellas.

clue.text: Assassin was at the front, honest!

parts.note: Gavrilo Princip shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914
to have been at the front is to have led

explanation.surface: A defence of a killer who led the charge, insisting he is honest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was at the front' sounds like the battlefield, given the 1914 assassin, but simply means LED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with firm moral standards who acts on them is upright and honest.

clue.text: Events guide hard going for 22 Down's amanuensis

indicators.note: going means the letter for hard is removed

parts.note: a What's On listing is a guide to local events
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A listings magazine loses its toughness, as the famous sleuth's writer-companion looks on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going' takes H out of WHAT'S ON. The doctor narrates the detective's adventures, hence amanuensis.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr John Watson records the cases in Conan Doyle's stories, acting as the detective's chronicler and scribe.

clue.text: Six tours sadly come to nothing for top player

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: sadly suggests things gone wrong, so the letters of tours are jumbled

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A star performer's six concert tours end in disappointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges the tours into RTUOS; 'come to' merely links it to the nothing that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer of outstanding technical skill, especially a musician, is a master player.

clue.text: Fiat oddly parked behind vehicle by junction

indicators.note: parked behind places the odd letters of Fiat after the vehicle

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: oddly takes the first and third letters of the car name

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as by in three by four

explanation.surface: A small Italian car is left behind another vehicle near a road junction.
explanation.walkthrough: Carfax is the crossroads at the centre of Oxford, where four main streets meet.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is a specific famous Oxford crossroads, and more generally a place where four roads meet.

clue.text: Cabinet backs section of Companies Act

indicators.note: backs says the hidden letters are read backwards
section of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A government Cabinet supports a clause of company legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'section of' finds ESAC across 'companiES ACt'; 'backs' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A display cabinet is a glass-fronted container, a piece of furniture also called a display case.

clue.text: Doctor inserts wad in poor condition

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A physician packs a wound with gauze while the patient is unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a physician but is a verb meaning tamper, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Shabbiness or cheap tattiness is a poor, run-down state, so the noun fits the phrase.

clue.text: It nips William, say, right on the rear

indicators.note: on the rear moves the letter for right to the back of the royal title

parts.note: Prince William is an example of a prince

explanation.surface: Something pinches Prince William, with a cheeky jab on the backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the rear' takes R from PRINCE and puts it at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A crab's claw or a gripping tool closes on things, so it is something that nips.

clue.text: Firm line adopted by annoyed comic author

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm

indicators.note: adopted by takes the line into the other word
comic means funny-looking, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A company's line is taken up by an irritated writer of comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adopted by' and 'comic' together make NANDOYLE from the line letter and the annoyed letters. 'comic author' looks like the definition, but 'comic' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle was the Scottish writer who created the great Baker Street detective.

clue.text: Malleable ring twisted around cube

parts.note: O is ring-shaped

indicators.note: around puts the twisted word about the cube

parts.note: bent means twisted out of shape
a die is a small cube used in games

explanation.surface: A soft metal ring is bent round a block.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twisted' looks like an anagram signal but is a plain synonym, and 'around' wraps it about the cube.
explanation.definitionFit: A compliant person is easily shaped by others, so malleable in character means dutiful and docile.

clue.text: Two metals generate dirt

parts.note: scandium, chemical symbol Sc, is the first of the two metals
the pair is written out with its joining word, as in 'this and that'
aluminium, chemical symbol Al, is the second of the two metals

explanation.surface: Combining a pair of metals produces muck.
explanation.walkthrough: The two metals are written out as a phrase, symbols joined by the word that links any pair: SC AND AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirt as in gossip or damaging revelations about someone, the sense of 'dishing the dirt'.

clue.text: Flyers provided with a uniform in a clapped-out van

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in puts the other pieces inside the jumbled van
clapped-out means worn out and battered, so the letters of van are rearranged

parts.note: provided that means if
taken as written
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Pilots in uniform travel in a broken-down old van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clapped-out' rearranges the van into VNA, and 'in' places the provided, a, uniform letters inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The collective term for the birds of a region; birds are the flyers of the animal world.

clue.text: It's read to divine crook in Bow

definitions.meaning: fortune tellers read the leaves left in a cup to predict the future
Cockney rhyming slang for thief; Bow is in London's East End, home of Cockneys

explanation.surface: A fortune teller reads the future of a criminal from the East End.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a fragment left in a teacup for reading fortunes and rhyming slang for a thief.

clue.text: Chose article on famous houses at home

indicators.note: in a down clue, on places the article above the rest

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: houses means contains, so the famous word holds the home word

parts.note: noted means famous
in means at home

explanation.surface: Someone picks an article about celebrity homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'houses' is a verb meaning contains, not the celebrities' homes; 'on' sets the article on top in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To anoint someone is to pick them out for office, so chosen and anointed are near synonyms.

clue.text: Fancy C-listers ringing Hoy for one!

indicators.note: ringing means surrounding, so the words enclose the answer's letters

explanation.surface: Minor celebrities surround a famous sportsman, with a fancy-dress air.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Chris Hoy is a British Olympic track champion; the letters run from 'fanCY' into 'C-LISTers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Chris Hoy, multiple Olympic gold medallist on the track, is an example of a bike racer.

clue.text: I refuse to accept bird's name

indicators.note: to accept means the refusal word takes in the bird

parts.note: to refuse is to deny
a tit is a small bird

explanation.surface: Someone declines to take on a bird's name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to accept' puts the bird inside the refusal word.
explanation.definitionFit: A name is what identifies who you are, so it stands for who someone is.

clue.text: Disgustingly dirty bottled whiskey that's typical of Wilde

indicators.note: bottled means held inside, so the jumbled letters enclose the other piece
disgustingly suggests a mess, so the letters of dirty are scrambled

parts.note: W is whiskey in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A grubby bottle of whiskey of the kind Oscar Wilde might have drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disgustingly' rearranges DIRTY to DRYIT, which has W 'bottled' inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde was famed for deadpan, ironic humour delivered with a straight face.

clue.text: Fox hounds bay

indicators.note: to fox is to confuse, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A fox is chased by a pack of baying hounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fox' looks like the hunted animal, and 'bay' like the hounds' cry, but 'Fox' is a verb meaning confuse, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hudson Bay is the vast inland sea in north-eastern Canada.

clue.text: Sleuth mainly begins probing parts of course

indicators.note: probing means pushing into, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: a golf course is made up of holes

indicators.note: begins takes the opening letter of the word mainly

explanation.surface: A detective mostly starts by investigating sections of a route.
explanation.walkthrough: M goes inside HOLES; a golf course has eighteen holes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock Holmes is fiction's most famous detective, the archetypal sleuth.

clue.text: Developer forged payroll log

indicators.note: forged means fabricated, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A property developer has falsified the payroll records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Developer' suggests property, but the answer is a chemical used to develop photographs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyrogallic acid was an early photographic developing agent, used to bring out images on plates.

clue.text: See 26
Sexton left out roast

indicators.note: out means the letter for left is removed

parts.note: Sexton Blake is a fictional detective of British pulp magazines

explanation.surface: A church sexton is excluded from the Sunday roast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sexton' looks like a church caretaker; it is the first name of the detective Sexton Blake, a long-running British pulp hero.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast and to bake both mean cooking food in an oven with dry heat.

clue.text: To which 22 Down applied "His Last Bow"?

definitions.text: To which 22 Down applied "His Last Bow"?

parts.words: To which 22 Down applied "His Last Bow"?
parts.note: His Last Bow is the title of a Conan Doyle story, but read literally it is a stroke of the bow on the detective's stringed instrument

explanation.surface: A question about where the detective's final story title came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Holmes famously plays the fiddle; a bow is drawn across its strings.
explanation.definitionFit: The detective plays this stringed instrument, and a bow is what is applied to it.

clue.text: Spotted group, a 10 for 22 Down

parts.note: spotted means covered in small specks or dots
a group of musicians, an ensemble

explanation.surface: A spotted group is a mystery for the great detective.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 Across is CASE and 22 Down is HOLMES: the answer is the title of one of his cases.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adventure of the Speckled Band is one of the best-known Sherlock Holmes short stories.
